sections.0.body.0.t: An eval is a software experiment. You assemble a dataset of prompts with the expected output, define a metric (heuristic, embedding or LLM judge) and run everything through a runner that scores each case and returns an average. When the average goes up, you know it improved. When it drops, you know it got worse, without needing to argue.

sections.0.body.1.t: Three pieces support everything: the dataset (input/expected pairs or production traces), the metric (how to compare output with expected) and the runner (the loop that calls the agent, captures the output, applies the metric and aggregates). The metric is where almost every team stumbles: the first version tends to be too vague and accepts anything.

sections.1.body.0.t: The dataset needs real coverage: easy cases (smoke), edge cases (contradiction in the history, a tool that fails) and adversarial cases (a malicious instruction embedded in a retrieved document). 50 well-chosen cases beat 5,000 template-generated cases. Coverage matters more than volume.

sections.1.body.1.t: The metric defines what 'good' is. Faithfulness asks whether the answer is faithful to the retrieved context (no invented sources). Relevance asks whether it answers what was asked. Groundedness asks whether every claim is supported by the context and was not made up by the model. Each metric becomes a deterministic function or a judge prompt; both live in the same file.

sections.1.body.2.t: The runner is the glue. It receives the dataset, walks through each case, calls the agent with a timeout, captures the output (and the chain of tool calls, if it is an agent), applies the metric and returns a report in JSON or CSV. It is the component that goes into CI.

sections.2.body.0.t: Before running 500 cases, it is worth running a single one and reading the result by eye. A case for a RAG agent on vacation policies might be:

sections.2.code.0.code.t:
id: ferias-elege-01
input:
  pergunta: "Can I sell 5 vacation days to pay for my health plan?"
  contexto_recuperado:
    - "Policy 7.2: selling up to 10 vacation days per year is allowed."
    - "Policy 4.1: the advance is deposited into the account holder's checking account."
expected:
  tem_que_dizer:
    - "Yes, selling up to 10 days is allowed"
  nao_pode_dizer:
    - "Selling vacation is prohibited"
metricas:
  - fidelidade: groundedness
  - relevancia: answer-covers-question
  - completude: contains-numeric-value

sections.3.body.0.t: Faithfulness (groundedness) compares each sentence of the answer with the retrieved context. If the model claims something with no support in the context, it loses points. It is the metric that catches hallucination earliest.

sections.3.body.1.t: Relevance measures whether the answer covers what was asked. An LLM judge with a binary rubric (answered / did not answer) already solves it. The catch is the technically correct answer that ignores the question, and the metric needs to catch that.

sections.3.body.2.t: Overall quality (helpfulness, completeness) aggregates everything: tone, clarity, usefulness. It tends to be the most subjective and where the human judge shines. Reserve it for small samples, not for 100% of the dataset.

sections.4.body.0.t: The skeleton below loads a case YAML, calls the agent, applies an LLM judge and returns a verdict. In production the runner is bigger (parallelism, cache, retries), but the format fits well in this document:

sections.5.body.0.t: Twice. Before the merge: the regression suite runs on every PR and blocks if it drops. After the merge: production samples are re-evaluated to detect drift (the model changed, retrieval degraded, prompt injection leaked).

sections.5.body.1.t: Without the second stage you end up in self-deception. Metrics that only look at the PR's history do not catch runtime regressions, and the defect shows up only when the user complains.

sections.5.heading.t: Where it fits in the pipeline

sections.6.bullets.0.t: replaces discussion with a number: 'faithfulness dropped 4 points' is an argument that closes a thread

sections.6.bullets.1.t: covers regressions invisible to the naked eye, especially in long tool calling chains

sections.6.bullets.2.t: generates a correctable dataset that the suite itself uses, becoming a virtuous improvement loop

sections.7.bullets.0.t: bad metrics start to deceive: an uncalibrated LLM judge becomes a rubber stamp that accepts anything

sections.7.bullets.1.t: a stalled dataset ages: the agent evolves, the suite does not, and the metric stops reflecting reality

sections.7.bullets.2.t: cost: running 500 cases with an LLM judge is billed per token, takes time and requires respecting the judge API's rate limit

short.t: dataset, metric and runner to measure quality

tagline.t: Evals are the harness that measures whether the answer is good: a dataset of examples, a metric (faithfulness, relevance, groundedness) and a runner that executes end to end. Without evals, improving an agent is guesswork and every tweak becomes routine.
